newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader sees "carnage" if referendum fails.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader sees "carnage" if referendum fails.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko urged Belarus to back him or face "carnage" as early voting began this weekend on a referendum he hopes will grant him new powers in the face of opposition from parliament.

"God forbid that we should lose. God forbid that I should fail to get support at the referendum. They (the opposition) will unleash carnage and dismiss me from power," he said in an interview on state television late on Saturday.
"I am scared to think what the opposition could do next. They know nothing but dirty tricks," he added.

Defying the constitution, parliament and electoral authorities, Lukashenko decreed the referendum, if approved, will give him a direct mandate to extend his term by more than two years and increase his sway over all branches of power.
Parliament, backed by the constitutional court, had voted that the referendum could only be advisory and have no legal force. But Lukashenko overturned this by decree last week.
The referendum is scheduled for November 24 but early voting began on November 9, though electoral officials said only a handful of voters had turned up by Sunday.
Lukashenko has vowed to dissolve any branch of power which interfered with the vote -- including parliament and the constitutional court.
That has raised the stakes in a row compared by some analysts to a legal stalemate in Russia in 1993, which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.
Lukashenko has faced criticism from the West for his increasingly authoritarian rule. He keeps a tight rein on the press and regularly dismisses constitutional court rulings.

The head of the constitutional court, Valery Tikhinya, said last week that Lukashenko could suffer a fate similar to that of Romanian dictator Nicolae Ceausescu -- shot during the revolution of 1989 -- or former South Korean leader Roh Tae-Woo, serving a 22-1/2 year prison sentence.
"Stop before it's too late. History has its precedents for such things -- Roh Tae-Woo in South Korea, Ceausescu in Romania or other dictators. There is always a finale," he said.

Voters face a confusing seven questions, including Lukashenko's draft constitution to boost his powers and another draft, proposed by legislators, which would scrap the presidency in its present form and strengthen parliamentary rule.
"Even with my higher education I do not understand the questions. So where does that leave the old women in the villages?" said Galina, 46, when asked how she would vote.
Lukashenko's draft is expected to do well. Television has broadcast repeated appeals to vote accompanied by a picture of a voting form filled out to back the president and oppose parliament.

The 42-year-old leader, a former collective farm boss, has broad support in rural Belarus. His anti-corruption, pro-Moscow stance won him a landslide victory in July 1994 in the republic of 10 million sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
Another question proposed by Lukashenko asks whether Belarus should continue to enforce the death penalty. He has said he wants the practice to continue.
Officials at one polling station said only two people had cast their ballots on Saturday, the first day of voting. Copies of the constitutional drafts were nowhere to be seen.
"We know nothing. We have no copies of the drafts. Maybe the head of the commission will bring them some time," one electoral official said with a shrug.
Correspondents noted some minor irregularities at polling stations. One foreign citizen was handed a ballot paper. Another voter was registered twice.
